    Downsampling with quality weights¶

    downsample aggregates 30 m pixels into coarse cells (about 1, 2 or 10 km) with quality weights, after chaining and re-referencing. Each cell gets a weighted mean or median, a sigma, the effective sample count, the share of the block that holds data and a quality score. to_points turns the cells into a point table for fits and GNSS comparison.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import disp_xr as dxr
from disp_xr.tutorial import make_disp_stack

folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "granules"
make_disp_stack(folder, "two_ministacks", shape=(128, 128))
ds = dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp(folder)).disp.rereference("median")
    import tempfile from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import disp_xr as dxr from disp_xr.tutorial import make_disp_stack folder = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "granules" make_disp_stack(folder, "two_ministacks", shape=(128, 128)) ds = dxr.chain(dxr.open_disp(folder)).disp.rereference("median")

    Aggregate¶

    Factor 9 turns 30 m into 270 m cells here (on a real frame use 33, 67 or 333). Odd factors keep each cell centre on a pixel centre. Weights default to quality_weights (similarity, coherence and inversion residuals), per epoch.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    coarse = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=9).compute()
print(dict(coarse.sizes), coarse.attrs["resolution"], "m")
print(list(coarse.data_vars)[:10])
    coarse = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=9).compute() print(dict(coarse.sizes), coarse.attrs["resolution"], "m") print(list(coarse.data_vars)[:10])
    {'time': 11, 'y': 15, 'x': 15} 270 m
['displacement', 'displacement_sigma', 'short_wavelength_displacement', 'short_wavelength_displacement_sigma', 'estimated_phase_quality', 'estimated_phase_quality_sigma', 'shp_counts', 'shp_counts_sigma', 'recommended_mask', 'water_mask']

):

    ax.set_title(title, loc="left")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
    last = {"time": -1} fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.6), layout="constrained") (ds.displacement.isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[0], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) (coarse.displacement.isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[1], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) (coarse.displacement_sigma.isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[2], cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) coarse.valid_fraction.isel(**last).plot.imshow(ax=axes[3], vmin=0, vmax=1) for ax, title in zip( axes, ("30 m", "270 m weighted mean", "cell sigma", "valid fraction") ): ax.set_title("") # drop xarray's automatic title ax.set_title(title, loc="left") ax.set_aspect("equal") plt.show()

    The low-coherence corner gets weight 0, so its cell has no value; the right edge cells extend past the frame (128 is not a multiple of 9) and their valid fraction shows how much of the block they hold. The sigma treats pixels as independent; spatially correlated errors make it too small at kilometre scales, which the next section fixes.

    Spatial variation within a cell¶

    sigma is the uncertainty of the cell value. How much the pixels differ inside the cell is a different question, answered with spread: the weighted standard deviation (std), the weighted RMS about the cell value (rmse), and the weighted median absolute deviation from the weighted median (mad), which outlier pixels (unwrapping errors, a building) barely move. All use the same weights as the cell value. With a weighted median and mad, every statistic of the cell is robust. For Gaussian noise the MAD is about 0.67 times the std, as in the maps below (1.4826 MAD estimates the std).

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    robust = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=9, stat="wmedian", spread=["std", "mad"]).compute()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6), layout="constrained")
(robust.displacement.isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow(
    ax=axes[0], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"}
)
for ax, name in zip(axes[1:], ("std", "mad")):
    (robust[f"displacement_{name}"].isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow(
        ax=ax, cmap="magma", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"}
    )
for ax, title in zip(
    axes,
    ("270 m weighted median", "within-cell weighted std", "within-cell weighted MAD"),
):
    ax.set_title("")  # drop xarray's automatic title
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
    robust = dxr.downsample(ds, factor=9, stat="wmedian", spread=["std", "mad"]).compute() fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.6), layout="constrained") (robust.displacement.isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[0], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) for ax, name in zip(axes[1:], ("std", "mad")): (robust[f"displacement_{name}"].isel(**last) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=ax, cmap="magma", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) for ax, title in zip( axes, ("270 m weighted median", "within-cell weighted std", "within-cell weighted MAD"), ): ax.set_title("") # drop xarray's automatic title ax.set_title(title, loc="left") ax.set_aspect("equal") plt.show()

    Sigma with spatially correlated errors¶

    InSAR errors (troposphere, unwrapping) are correlated over kilometres, so averaging 81 pixels does not divide the noise by 9. Following xDEM (Hugonnet et al. 2022), estimate a variogram on a residual field (stable ground, or data minus a model), fit it, and pass it to downsample. Here the residual is synthetic: correlated noise with a 900 m range, 2 mm correlated and 1 mm white.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    import numpy as np  # noqa: E402

from disp_xr.tutorial import correlated_noise  # noqa: E402

noise = correlated_noise(
    (128, 128), correlation_range=900, sill=(2e-3) ** 2, nugget=(1e-3) ** 2
)
residual = ds.displacement.isel(time=-1).copy(data=noise)
empirical = dxr.empirical_variogram(residual)
model = dxr.fit_variogram(empirical, ("exponential",))
print(model)

h = np.linspace(1, float(empirical.distance.max()), 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.4), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(empirical.distance, empirical.gamma * 1e6, "o", label="empirical")
ax.plot(h, model.gamma(h) * 1e6, label="fitted model")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="distance (m)", ylabel="semivariance (mm$^2$)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
    import numpy as np # noqa: E402 from disp_xr.tutorial import correlated_noise # noqa: E402 noise = correlated_noise( (128, 128), correlation_range=900, sill=(2e-3) ** 2, nugget=(1e-3) ** 2 ) residual = ds.displacement.isel(time=-1).copy(data=noise) empirical = dxr.empirical_variogram(residual) model = dxr.fit_variogram(empirical, ("exponential",)) print(model) h = np.linspace(1, float(empirical.distance.max()), 300) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.4), layout="constrained") ax.plot(empirical.distance, empirical.gamma * 1e6, "o", label="empirical") ax.plot(h, model.gamma(h) * 1e6, label="fitted model") ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="distance (m)", ylabel="semivariance (mm$^2$)") ax.legend() plt.show()
    VariogramModel(nugget=9.003268065236777e-07, components=(('exponential', 2.900470225785386e-06, 571.4754068644789),))
    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    noisy = ds.assign(displacement=ds.displacement + noise)
corr = dxr.downsample(noisy, factor=9, variogram={"displacement": model}).compute()
print(
    "median cell sigma, pixels independent:",
    f"{float(corr.displacement_sigma.median()) * 1000:.2f} mm;",
    "with the variogram:",
    f"{float(corr.displacement_sigma_corr.median()) * 1000:.2f} mm",
)
    noisy = ds.assign(displacement=ds.displacement + noise) corr = dxr.downsample(noisy, factor=9, variogram={"displacement": model}).compute() print( "median cell sigma, pixels independent:", f"{float(corr.displacement_sigma.median()) * 1000:.2f} mm;", "with the variogram:", f"{float(corr.displacement_sigma_corr.median()) * 1000:.2f} mm", )
    median cell sigma, pixels independent: 0.23 mm; with the variogram: 1.22 mm

    The variogram sigma is several times larger: neighbouring pixels share most of their error. n_eff_corr is the effective number of independent pixels per cell. The model holds for every epoch; estimate it on the epoch or the velocity residual you care about.

    Hexagonal cells¶

    downsample_hex groups pixels into hexagons instead of squares: all six neighbors are equidistant, so the sampling is more isotropic. The lattice is anchored at the CRS origin, so overlapping frames of one UTM zone share cells. A spacing of 1.0746 times a square's side gives the same area; here 290 m hexagons next to the 270 m squares. The statistics are the same, and the result is a point table like to_points.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    hexes = dxr.downsample_hex(ds, spacing=290).compute()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained")
dxr.plot.plot_map(coarse, ax=axes[0], title="270 m squares")
dxr.plot.plot_hex(hexes, ax=axes[1], title="290 m hexagons")
plt.show()
print(hexes.sizes["point"], "hexagons;", int(hexes.pixels.median()), "pixels each")
    hexes = dxr.downsample_hex(ds, spacing=290).compute() fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained") dxr.plot.plot_map(coarse, ax=axes[0], title="270 m squares") dxr.plot.plot_hex(hexes, ax=axes[1], title="290 m hexagons") plt.show() print(hexes.sizes["point"], "hexagons;", int(hexes.pixels.median()), "pixels each")
    246 hexagons; 80 pixels each

    H3 global cells (grid="h3", the hex extra) line up across frames and UTM zones, so cells from neighboring frames merge by their h3_cell id. to_geodataframe returns the cells as polygons for GIS tools.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    h3_cells = dxr.downsample_hex(ds, grid="h3", resolution=9).compute()
gdf = dxr.to_geodataframe(h3_cells)
print(h3_cells.sizes["point"], "H3 cells at resolution 9")
gdf[["h3_cell", "displacement", "n_eff", "geometry"]].head()
    h3_cells = dxr.downsample_hex(ds, grid="h3", resolution=9).compute() gdf = dxr.to_geodataframe(h3_cells) print(h3_cells.sizes["point"], "H3 cells at resolution 9") gdf[["h3_cell", "displacement", "n_eff", "geometry"]].head()

    Quadtree¶

    quadtree keeps large cells where the data are smooth and splits them where they vary. Levels are factor-2 cells from 2^min_level pixels; a cell splits while its score is above the threshold and its four children keep enough reliable pixels. With metric="displacement" the score is the RMS weighted spread of the pixels in the cell, in meters. to_raster paints the leaves back on the 30 m grid.

    Which to use: in the T29 trade study (three DISP-S1 frames, report), the regular grid of downsample reconstructed the 30 m field better than any quadtree with the same number of points, and agreed better with GNSS except across a creeping fault. Use the grid by default and the quadtree for sharp, local gradients. The quadtree's default metric is "structure", which splits where the four children differ by more than their noise; the displacement metric used here reads in meters and, on real frames, splits noisy cells first. For Cal/Val accuracy runs, a stricter coherence floor in the weights (dxr.quality_weights(ds, floors={"temporal_coherence": 0.8})) agreed better with GNSS, at the cost of 12 to 39% of the pixels.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    tree = dxr.quadtree(
    ds, threshold=0.002, metric="displacement", min_level=2, max_level=5
)
leaves = tree.points.compute()
print(leaves.level.to_series().value_counts().sort_index().rename("leaves"))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained")
(ds.displacement.isel(time=-1) * 1000).plot.imshow(
    ax=axes[0], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"}
)
(tree.to_raster("displacement") * 1000).plot.imshow(
    ax=axes[1], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"}
)
for ax, title in zip(axes, ("30 m", "quadtree leaves")):
    ax.set_title("")  # drop xarray's automatic title
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
    tree = dxr.quadtree( ds, threshold=0.002, metric="displacement", min_level=2, max_level=5 ) leaves = tree.points.compute() print(leaves.level.to_series().value_counts().sort_index().rename("leaves")) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), layout="constrained") (ds.displacement.isel(time=-1) * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[0], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) (tree.to_raster("displacement") * 1000).plot.imshow( ax=axes[1], cmap="RdBu_r", cbar_kwargs={"label": "mm"} ) for ax, title in zip(axes, ("30 m", "quadtree leaves")): ax.set_title("") # drop xarray's automatic title ax.set_title(title, loc="left") ax.set_aspect("equal") plt.show()
